```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(eval = FALSE)
```

This article shows the `inedemogR` code behind each figure in the
[Gallery](gallery.html): retrieving the data and computing the indicators.
The chunks are not run here because they need the live INE API. Styling
(colours, labels, layout) is plain `ggplot2`, `sf` and `patchwork` code and
is left out.

## Setup and caching

Every figure starts from the same few downloads. Pass a `cache_dir` so that
each table is fetched from INE once and read from disk afterwards; the first
run takes several minutes.

```{r}
library(inedemogR)
library(dplyr)

cache <- "cache"
pop        <- get_ine_population(cache_dir = cache)$data
births     <- get_ine_births(cache_dir = cache)$data
births_age <- get_ine_births_by_age(n_periods = 30, cache_dir = cache)$data
deaths     <- get_ine_deaths(cache_dir = cache)
```

All four return one row per province, year and (where relevant) single year
of age, with `female`, `male` and `total` columns.

## Natural change by province

Crude birth and death rates per 1,000 residents, then their difference.

```{r}
rni <- rate_of_natural_increase(
  crude_birth_rate(births, pop),
  crude_death_rate(deaths$data_provinces, pop)
)
rni_2024 <- filter(rni, year == 2024)
```

`get_ine_geo("province")` returns the province polygons (with the Canary
Islands moved next to the peninsula), ready to join and draw with
`ggplot2::geom_sf()`.

## Spain as a whole: pool, then compute

The figures for all of Spain pool the counts over the 52 provinces first and
compute the rate after. Averaging the provincial rates would weight a small
province the same as Madrid.

```{r}
spain <- function(df, cols) {
  df |>
    summarise(across(all_of(cols), sum), .by = c(year, age, any_of("age_group"))) |>
    mutate(nuts3_code = "ES", province_name = "Spain")
}
```

## Total fertility rate by province

Age-specific fertility rates use births by single year of the mother's age
over mid-year women (the mean of the 1 January stocks of year *t* and *t* + 1),
so the population must include the year after the last one you want.

```{r}
years <- c(2000, 2024)
b <- filter(births_age, year %in% years)
p <- filter(pop, year %in% c(years, years + 1))

tfr_prov  <- total_fertility_rate(age_specific_fertility_rate(b, p))
tfr_spain <- total_fertility_rate(age_specific_fertility_rate(
  spain(b, c("female", "total")), spain(p, "female")
))
```

## Population pyramid

`plot_population_pyramid()` adds up the provinces and returns a `ggplot`
object, so further layers (here the 2002 outline) go on with `+`.

```{r}
plot_population_pyramid(pop, 2025)
```

## Age-specific fertility rates over time

Same function as for the TFR, for all of Spain and every year. For five-year
groups, add up births and women within each group and divide; do not average
the single-year rates.

```{r}
asfr <- age_specific_fertility_rate(
  spain(filter(births_age, year >= 1996), c("female", "total")),
  spain(pop, "female")
)
tfr <- total_fertility_rate(asfr)

asfr5 <- asfr |>
  mutate(group = sprintf("%d-%d", age %/% 5 * 5, age %/% 5 * 5 + 4)) |>
  summarise(asfr = 1000 * sum(births) / sum(women), .by = c(group, year))
```

## Lexis surface of mortality

Exposure follows the Human Mortality Database protocol: Lexis-triangle
deaths combined with the 1 January stocks. Death rates by single age and year
come out as `mx_1x1`, which `plot_lexis_diagram()` draws for one sex.

```{r}
d <- deaths$data_provinces |> filter(year >= min(pop$year))
d_es   <- spain(d, c("female", "male", "total"))
pop_es <- spain(pop, c("female", "male", "total"))

mx <- compute_death_rates(d_es, compute_exposure(pop_es, d_es)$data)$mx_1x1
plot_lexis_diagram(mx, province = "Spain", sex = "female")
```

Before 2002 INE published population above age 84 only as one open group,
so those cells have no rate; the Gallery figure shows them in grey.
